title: Act V, Scene III

teacherSummary.text: Paris mourns at the tomb; Romeo arrives, kills him, and drinks poison beside Juliet. The Friar arrives as Juliet wakes; she refuses to leave and stabs herself. The watch gathers; the Friar confesses; Montague and Capulet reconcile.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this play is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Act V, Scene III,” how does Shakespeare show the tomb? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Act V, Scene III, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of the tomb? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the irony in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Act V, Scene III develops the idea of the tomb. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of irony and plot shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act V, Scene III (where it begins, turns and ends) and its irony shape the reader's understanding of the tomb. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act V, Scene III suggests about the tomb. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's irony and plot), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses irony in Act V, Scene III to complicate the reader's understanding of the tomb. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act V, Scene III within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of the tomb responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act V, Scene III alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of the tomb follows or bends those conventions, using the irony as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act V, Scene III and its treatment of the tomb. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's irony and plot, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act V, Scene III as evidence for a larger claim about the tomb in Romeo and Juliet. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act V, Scene III as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of the tomb. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Romeo and Juliet.

I hear some noise. Lady, come from that nest
Of death, contagion, and unnatural sleep:

Among a sisterhood of holy nuns:

Come, go, good Juliet noise again, I dare no longer stay.

symbolsAndMotifs.name: light and dark
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: The lovers describe each other as light in darkness (torches, sun, stars, lightning), yet they can meet only at night, and daylight brings danger. In this scene: “Enter Paris, and his Page bearing flowers and a torch” (Act V, Scene III, speech (speech 0)).
symbolsAndMotifs.quote: Enter Paris, and his Page bearing flowers and a torch

symbolsAndMotifs.name: fate and the stars
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: From "star-cross'd" in the Prologue to Romeo's "I defy you, stars," the lovers feel steered by fortune, while the plot shows human choices and accidents. In this scene: “pry / In what I further shall intend to do, / By heaven, I will tear thee joint by joint / And strew this hungry” (Act V, Scene III, Romeo (speech 4)).

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.

Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Romeo dies by poison and Juliet by a dagger; Paris is killed. Use the safe-messaging script; discuss the Prince's verdict and the waste of young lives, not methods.
contentNotes.studentPreview: The ending shows three deaths, two by suicide. Support is available if this is hard to read.
contentNotes.suggestedLanguage: “Who does the Prince say is responsible, and do you agree?”

safeMessaging.teacherScript: Discuss the character's despair and what the text does with it; do not dwell on methods. Before the lesson, remind students that support is available and how to reach the counselor. Check in privately with any student who seems affected and follow your school's referral protocol.
safeMessaging.studentResource: If you or someone you know is struggling or thinking about suicide, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, U.S.) or talk with a school counselor today.
safeMessaging.counselorPrompt: Let a counselor know in advance that this scene is being taught.
